extracted.intended_audience: students and authors of mathematical / computer-science papers and talks (e.g., Don Knuth's students)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and standards for preparing mathematical/computer-science papers, proofs, illustrations, and presentations — covering notation, diagrams, examples, and interactions with editors. Targeted at students and technical authors preparing homework, papers, or magazine articles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams: keep small when possible
rubrics_metrics.description: Diagrams are good if they are kept small.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Small diagrams are preferred; fold-outs are acceptable for complex comparisons but generally keep illustrations compact so they fit easily in prose and cause less production trouble.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams: include detail for those who want it
rubrics_metrics.description: Include sufficient minutiae for readers who want to see the details, but organize so those details can be ignored by readers who don't.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don disagreed with a referee who complained a figure was too detailed, arguing that detail can serve readers who want it while being skippable for others. Balance completeness and readability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Illustrations preparation cost
rubrics_metrics.description: The amount of work preparing a paper for publication is proportional to the cube of the number of illustrations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Minimize unnecessary illustrations since each additional figure can greatly increase preparation workload and typesetting complexity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Color use: talks vs papers
rubrics_metrics.description: Color can be used effectively in talks, but usually not in papers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reserve four-color (or colored) illustrations for presentations; be cautious using color in printed papers due to production constraints and cost.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place final text opposite diagrams
rubrics_metrics.description: Arrange final text opposite the diagrams to which it refers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When possible, put explanatory text on the page facing the figure to improve readability and reduce cross-page searching.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use real data rather than cooked-up sample data
rubrics_metrics.description: It is better to use 'real' data than 'sample data' that have been cooked up solely to use as an example.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select genuine test paragraphs, datasets, or examples to illustrate algorithm behavior; e.g., using a Grimms' Fairy Tale paragraph as test data for line-breaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide numerical evidence (histograms/tables) but note bias
rubrics_metrics.description: Use histograms or numerical tables to illustrate frequency or performance, but acknowledge biases in how the data were produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don printed histograms showing how often TEX generates distorted lines and explained that his rewrites biased the results; report such biases when they exist.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tables and numerical tables can convey otherwise non-graphical ideas
rubrics_metrics.description: Numerical tables sometimes present ideas that can't be demonstrated graphically.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use tables when they reveal patterns (e.g., oscillating numbers) not easily shown by diagrams; don't dismiss numeric tables as inherently unenlightening.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams to explain algorithms (graph representation)
rubrics_metrics.description: When describing algorithms, translate the problem to a well-understood representation (e.g., graph nodes as break points, edges labeled with demerits) to leverage standard techniques.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: model line-breaking as a least-cost path problem with nodes at possible break points and edge costs as demerits; then apply search techniques.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explain algorithmic trade-offs (deemerit cutoffs, missed solutions)
rubrics_metrics.description: Discuss algorithmic heuristics and their trade-offs, such as demerit cutoffs that improve speed but may miss some optimal solutions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be explicit about what approximations or cutoffs do (e.g., limiting nodes per level speeds algorithm but may skip solutions where one distorted line allows others to be perfect).

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams can make opaque prose clear
rubrics_metrics.description: If an account is opaque in prose, a diagram can often make the idea clear.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use diagrams to show structure and relationships when textual descriptions are hard to parse; don't over-rely on prose alone for spatial/structural ideas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Diagrams: fold-out illustrations for complex comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Large fold-out illustrations are useful for complex comparisons (e.g., sort-on-tapes performance) that involve overlaps, rewinds, buffering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For multi-dimensional or timeline-dependent comparisons where space is required, a large fold-out can capture subtleties conventional analysis misses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nested diagrams for hierarchical structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Use nested boxes (boxes within boxes) as an alternative to tree diagrams to represent hierarchical or nested structures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: ATNs for parsing or Winograd's nested-diagram use; choose the diagram type that best conveys structure to your audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of scattergrams / glyphs for multivariate data
rubrics_metrics.description: Several numeric dimensions can control features of glyphs (e.g., smiley faces) to exploit human sensitivity to facial/numeric nuances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Map multiple variables to perceivable glyph attributes if the audience can read such encodings; be cautious about ambiguous encodings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Listing events vs diagrams for asynchronous processes
rubrics_metrics.description: For asynchronous processes, a listing of events may be the clearest way to convey essential features when a neat diagram is elusive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a diagram can't capture complexity cleanly (e.g., Caltech elevator states), prefer an ordered event listing to preserve clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledgements and authorship ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Properly acknowledge contributors and co-authors; do not omit co-authors in haste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Young authors often overlook acknowledgments. Don admitted failing to credit students who contributed ideas and illustrations; avoid this anti-pattern.

rubrics_metrics.name: Minimize subscripts and subscripted superscripts
rubrics_metrics.description: Aim for notation that needs no double subscripts or subscripted superscripts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For clarity and readability, recast proofs to eliminate nested indices; the homework assignment explicitly required removing subscripted subscripts/superscripts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hold back before enumerating elements
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid immediately introducing enumerated notation; you can often say 'S is countable' instead of writing S = {s1, s2, ...}.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Using words rather than notation can simplify exposition and reduce notational clutter where the exact enumeration is unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor proofs into subgoals
rubrics_metrics.description: Factor a proof into parts: one that establishes a crucial subgoal and another that applies it to finish the argument.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factoring reduces cognitive load by creating a simple interface between pieces and makes proofs easier to follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: State the overarching proof technique to orient readers
rubrics_metrics.description: Tell the reader what kind of technique the proof uses (e.g., 'essentially a diagonalization technique') to provide orientation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A brief statement of technique offers immediate context and helps readers understand the structure and expected moves in the proof.

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide initialization / handle special cases for exposition
rubrics_metrics.description: Ensure exposition handles base cases or initialization explicitly (e.g., single out k=1) to aid readers unaccustomed to empty constraints.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A grader objected that an omitted initialization made the exposition harder to read; including such concessions improves clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer words over heavy notation when clearer
rubrics_metrics.description: Use plain English rather than elaborate notation when it improves understandability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Several student solutions used words in place of complicated correspondences, reducing notational overhead and making the proof easier to read.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose 'real' illustrative examples for algorithms and performance comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Select representative, realistic examples for demonstrating algorithm behavior (e.g., running the same 16 numbers through many sorts).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a consistent running example across multiple algorithms to allow direct, comparable graphical presentations of behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Find apt quotations to frame chapters or sections
rubrics_metrics.description: Use quotations that are apposite, beautiful, or memorable to open or conclude chapters; avoid pretentious quotation intended to show off learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Search Bartlett, OED, concordances, or online corpora; quoting oneself or obscure sources is acceptable if genuinely appropriate. Avoid gratuitous quotation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interact with editors: expect edits and request proofs
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect editorial changes when submitting to magazines (e.g., Scientific American); request galley proofs when technical/typographical content is heavy.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared to defend technical choices, check proofs carefully (important for mathematics), and recognize that some editorial changes may improve or degrade your exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Caption typesetting constraints and final-line fitting
rubrics_metrics.description: Some publications determine caption linebreaks by hand and may adjust wording to make the final line end exactly at the right margin.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be prepared for copy editors to rewrite captions for fit; small wording changes (removing 'the', rephrasing) are used to achieve neat typesetting.
